speechtext: Hon. members have been making some inquiries respecting the adjournment at Easter time for the vacation that is customarily taken during that season. speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROPOSED DATES

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROPOSED DATES
speechtext:
I should like to announce to the house that last week I sent a letter to the several provincial premiers proposing that a dominion-provincial conference on fiscal relations be held in Ottawa on July 25, 26 and 27 next, if these dates are generally acceptable to the various premiers.
Hon. members will recall that the Minister of Finance, at the meeting of the dominion-provincial committee of ministers of finance and provincial treasurers in Ottawa in October last, announced that the federal government intended to convene a plenary dominion-provincial conference in mid-1960 the purpose of which would be the discussing of the fiscal arrangements between the dominion and the provinces to follow the present tax-sharing arrangements, which will end on March 31, 1962.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROPOSED DATES
speechtext: With respect to the announcement with regard to a federal-provincial conference, which also had been forecast, it would be interesting to learn-and perhaps the Prime Minister could tell us now in view of previous statements that have been made on the matter-what will be the position of the municipalities at this conference.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROPOSED DATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that the Prime Minister has announced that the federal-provincial conference will be held in Ottawa. I think such a conference is most essential not only because the agreements are coming to an end, as the Prime Minister has said, on March 31, 1962, but because there are many urgent and pressing fiscal policies with which the provinces wish to deal at this time, regarding the solution of which the federal government can no doubt be of help.
I am pleased that the announcement is a firm one, and does not depend on whether or not the house is in session. I remember that on a former occasion the Minister of Finance said that such a conference could not be held with parliament in session. I do not think there is any need for one to bar the other. I am glad the announcement has been made even though I anticipate that the house may still be in session.

Continental Air Defence Policy NATIONAL DEFENCE

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I ask leave to move the adjournment of the house under standing order 26 for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the lack of adequate consultation between Canada and the United States, as revealed in statements made by the Minister of National Defence on and since Friday last, over the basic change made by the government of the United States in continental air defence policy, together with the decision of the minister to continue unchanged Canadian expenditures on a weapon for which a drastic cut has been proposed in the United States defence budget.
In speaking to this motion, Mr. Speaker, I do not of course have to do more than mention the importance of the subject with which it deals. I realize that under the standing order in question the matter must be not only important, but the discussion of it should be justified on the ground of urgency.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that statements which have been made in this house and outside the house by the minister and representative of the government have created a state of confusion, misunderstanding, and anxiety in the country which does make it urgent that this matter should be cleared up at the earliest possible date, and that one aspect of this confusion and anxiety-

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I do not want to interrupt the Leader of the Opposition, Your Honour, but he does not have to proceed with his argument to convince us that we desire an acceptance of this motion. He need not continue in that direction at all. We will be most happy to have and welcome the opportunity for a discussion of this question to remove misapprehensions and misinterpretations which have taken place over it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
If there are no hon. members who wish to present a contrary view, then my task is simply one of recognizing the will of the house. I will read the proposed subject matter upon which the Leader of the Opposition asks leave to move the adjournment of the house. It is in these terms:
I ask leave to move the adjournment of the house under standing order 26 for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the lack of adequate consultation between Canada and the United States, as revealed in statements made by the Minister of National Defence on and since Friday last, on the basic change made by the government of the United States in continental air defence policy, together

with the decision of the minister to continue unchanged Canadian expenditures on a weapon for which a drastic cut has been proposed in the United States defence budget.
Has the hon. member leave to move the motion?

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Agreed.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
In moving the adjournment of the house in order to discuss this matter, I do so not only because of the vital importance of the question of continental defence to every Canadian, but also because of our inability in this house to secure from the government any clear statement of defence policy, more particularly of continental defence policy.
This matter was brought up on this side in the debate on the address. I referred to it at some length on that occasion, as did other members of the official opposition. On that occasion the Minister of National Defence did not take advantage of the opportunity which was afforded to him of discussing this subject, a subject so very much in the minds of Canadians at this time, namely the defence of Canada and the defence of peace. Nor did any other member of the government discuss this question of defence policy and, more particularly, continental defence policy; neither have we had any such discussion in the house since that time.
It will be recalled that we had hoped-* and, indeed, I expressed this hope in the very first question I asked on the opening day of this session-that the question of defence could be submitted to a small committee of this house where it could be examined from the foundation, and where the whole concept and strategy of defence could be considered; where experts could be sent for, and where the kind of discussion which it seems to me the seriousness of the defence situation at this time warrants could have taken place quite irrespective of what may have been the practice in the house in previous years in discussing this subject.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I rise on a point of order. The hon. gentleman is repeating in almost identical terms what he said on a previous occasion. One might almost conclude that he was reading from the same document he used when he was discussing the motion to set up the committee-

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I was quite happy for a discussion to take place on the subject matter of the motion for the reason that was given in the motion on this occasion, but I submit that when the adjournment is moved for a given purpose the discussion should be
limited to what is contained in the motion for adjournment which has been moved.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Perhaps I should read to the house the limitations which do exist on a debate of this kind, as set out in standing order No. 26, subsection (6):
(6) The right to move the adjournment of the house for the above purposes is subject to the following restrictions:
(a)	not more than one such motion can be made at the same sitting;
(b)	not more than one matter can be discussed on the same motion;
I may have been a bit hasty in accepting this proposal as it is because there seem to be two matters raised, first the lack of adequate consultation between Canada and the United States, and second, the decision of the minister to continue unchanged Canadian expenditures on a weapon for which a drastic cut has been proposed in the United States defence budget.
As the matter of consultation is something in the past with respect to this item, I take it that the debate basically is on the decision of the minister to continue unchanged Canadian expenditures on a weapon for which a drastic cut has been proposed in the United States defence budget. That is the one matter which can be discussed on the motion. The standing order goes on to say:
(c)	the motion must not revive discussion on a matter which has been discussed in the same session:
(d)	the motion must not anticipate a matter which has been previously appointed for consideration by the house, or with reference to which a notice of motion has been previously given and not withdrawn:
Paragraph (e) which states that the motion must not raise a question of privilege is not relevant in this instance, but the succeeding paragraph reads:
(f) the discussion under the motion must not raise any question which, according to the standing orders of the house, can only be debated on a distinct motion under notice.
With those limitations before hon. members the subject to be discussed, I take it, is the decision of the minister to continue unchanged the Canadian expenditures on a weapon for which a drastic cut has been proposed in the United States defence budget.

Mr. Speaker, if I may say a word on the point of order, I submit with respect that you have already allowed this motion to be presented for discussion, and therefore it is rather difficult now to attempt to limit the discussion on the motion to only one part of it, namely the decision of the minister to continue unchanged Canadian expenditures, when in
Continental Air Defence Policy fact you yourself have said there are two parts to the motion, the first relating to the lack of adequate consultation.
While the lack of adequate consultation is a circumstance surrounding the events of last week, I would suggest to Your Honour that it raises something of fundamental importance, namely whether or not there are facilities that are being used for consultation between Canada and the United States. Even though the allowing of remarks concerning the motion as it now stands would rightly limit the discussion in the house, I suggest that you should allow discussion on the motion as it is framed not just part of it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Dealing with the point which the hon. member for Assiniboia has made, I am quite content with the view he expresses. The consultation which is referred to in this motion for adjournment, of course, is consultation with respect to this particular weapons program, so in essence what we are discussing is the decision of the government with respect to this particular weapon and the exchange by consultation with the United States with respect to this weapon.

Mr. Speaker, I gather that you have agreed to the discussion of these two matters referred to in the motion. While I realize that normally in a motion of this kind only one subject is put forward, I think it is also stated in Erskine May that if two matters are related to each other, Speakers in the past have permitted a discussion of the two related matters. Therefore I take it I am at liberty to discuss consultation between Canada and the United States in the field of continental defence policy, and also the expenditures on the Bomarc B weapon which is part of our weapons system and as such has a bearing on continental defence policy and on the organization of that continental defence policy. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I hope to keep my remarks within the limits of these two subjects.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
May I say this before the Leader of the Opposition proceeds. A discussion of consultation between Canada and the United States with respect to matters other than the Bomarc, which is the weapon referred to, would seem to me to be beyond the scope of the debate. In that sense there is really only one subject before the house, namely the government's policy with respect to this weapon and the development of that policy in consultation with the United States.
The motion is, of course, a motion to adjourn the house, and its interpretation is related to this document. I expect hon. members will keep to the purpose as we have narrowed it down.

Continental Air Defence Policy

Mr. Speaker, these two questions are related to each other. One has to do with consultation with the United States in respect of this particular weapon as part of our continental air defence, and the other with the expenditure of money on this particular weapon which is a part of our continental weapons system. Those are the two subjects, and in bringing this matter forward I had not anticipated that I would not be able to speak a length a least on the background leading up to this particular consultation and those particular expenditures. Because, Mr. Speaker, the basis of this motion is to be found in the statements made by the Minister of National Defence in this house last Friday at six o'clock, and the bearing of that particular statement, which deals with both those matters, on what the minister had said in this house only a few hours before, on Friday morning.
Consultation, Mr. Speaker, if there was consultation, which took place in regard to this matter it was a form of consultation the results of which had not been made known in any way, shape or form to this parliament while it was going on. This, Mr. Speaker, is surely an indication of the inadequacy of the present position of our defence arrangements with the United States of America. Not only are we to be put in a position where we are to continue to spend money on a weapon which is being discarded by the United States defence services-
No.
Where do you get that?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: That is not right.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

From the minister's own statement made in this house last Friday I will be able to show conclusively that it is right. The Minister of Public Works interjects and says that is not right. Let the minister get up and explain why the United States government has cut-
As soon as you sit down I will.

-the appropriation from $430 million to $50 million. If this does not represent a loss of confidence in a particular weapon, what can represent a loss of confidence?
In any event, there is no doubt that so far as consultation is concerned, we have built up over the years a system of consultation between the government in Ottawa and the government in Washington on defence and other matters. I suppose when NORAD was established by this government-a continental

defence organization without any real connection with NATO-one of the reasons it was not brought under NATO control in any effective way was, no doubt, that it would help to develop a better system of consultation between Canada and the United States in defence matters by the establishment of this continental defence arrangement which we know as NORAD. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, surely we in this house had some reason to believe that if there were in fact consultations going on between the two governments in regard to continental defence policy concerning this and other weapons, the house would have some information in regard to them, in regard to the decision taken by the government of Canada on this matter.
One of our complaints-and one of the reasons we brought this motion forward at this time, Mr. Speaker-is that if there was such consultation, there has been no suggestion to that end made at any time in this house during this session, in spite of efforts on our part to try to get from spokesmen of the government some statement about national defence, some statement about the results of this consultation, something about what was going on. We could not do that by setting up a committee because the government was not prepared to agree to any committee except one to discuss past expenditures. We have been questioning the minister, up until last Friday, as to what was going on in these consultations if they were being held in respect of this particular weapon which, once the Canadian-produced Arrow was destroyed, was apparently the new weapon on which continental defence policy was based, the Bomarc B, along with continental defence squadrons equipped with CF-100 airplanes.
We have, therefore, these two Canadian elements of continental defence. We have the Bomarc missile and we have the CF-100 interceptor squadrons. The minister himself said in 1957 that the CF-100 was obsolete. The Bomarc, which was to take the place of the Arrow, as the minister has also said on many occasions and which is quite true, will have no value in action against a missile. The minister has also said that missiles are becoming the main threat. He has not been so conclusive about the effectiveness of the Bomarc B against the supersonic bomber with which the Russian air force is now equipped. But its effectiveness, even if it were developed according to plan and operated according to plan, would be very doubtful indeed against even that kind of threat.
The minister has, in the past, stated that these interceptor planes and missiles would be able to engage and perhaps knock down

some enemy bombers. We could not count on too much in that respect. Nevertheless these are the weapons on which we have decided to base our continental defence policy, along with the CF-lOO's which, according to the minister, were obsolete two years ago. So we have a right to expect that consultation would be going on with the United States in regard to the effectiveness of this missile system and its ground environmental control system, which apparently is also now to be changed, and the possibility of maintaining interceptor squadrons of a type which would be presumably more effective than the CF-100, if such squadrons are to be retained along with the Bomarc in our continental system.
We have not at any time this session been able to get any information of any substantive character on these matters from the minister. We have asked questions; we have tried to bring the matters forward, and we have tried to set up a committee; but we did not learn, until I think it was Friday afternoon, that presumably as a result of consultation, the United States was to issue a statement that the whole basis of continental United States policy was going to be changed.
In the morning, Mr. Speaker, we asked the minister some questions about the reports in the newspapers to the effect that this had been decided. We were told in the morning -this was only a few hours before the minister's statement in the afternoon-that these were merely newspaper reports and we should not worry about them, we should not base any of our statements on reports of that kind. I think the expression the minister used was that they were merely speculative press reports; that remark can be found on page 2446 of Hansard. Yet we have learned since that on the day before, on Thursday of last week, the executive part of the government of the United States, presumably the defence department, had recommended to the appropriations committee of the United States house of representatives a transfer of funds which were to have been devoted to the production of these weapons to be used for other purposes which would increase the deterrent strength of continental defence, perhaps at the sacrifice of the more conventional points of defence.
This was confirmed by the minister himself in the statement which he gave to the house on Friday afternoon at six o'clock. I read from his statement:
The proposed transfer of funds was submitted In classified detail to the house appropriations committee in executive session on March 24, 1960.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, if that statement was made to the United States house committee
Continental Air Defence Policy on Thursday, March 24, the minister must have known about it if there was anything approaching adequate consultation. This must have been going on for weeks, and surely the minister must have known that the United States government had come to its own conclusions in regard to continental air defence, which conclusions were bound to have had an important effect on Canadian defence, if there is any such thing as Canadian defence apart from the defence of peace and the defence of the continent. Yet we got no reply from the minister in respect to questions we asked on this subject last week.
Now, on this question of consultation, this is what is included in the statement read by the minister on Friday night at six o'clock and this is the last paragraph of the statement:
Included in the revised air defence budget are provisions for SAGE direction and control in Canada. The Canadian Minister of National Defence has been kept fully informed throughout development of the air force's modified air defence plan.
Well, Mr. Speaker, there is a great deal of difference between the United States keeping a minister in the Canadian government informed about what is being done in regard to continental air defence, and consulting with the Canadian government in respect of joint continental air defence in a way which would make it possible for the Canadian government to express some views and to have some weight. If the latter kind of consultation were going on it is surprising indeed, in view of what the minister had to say on Friday morning, that at six o'clock that evening he could give a statement of this kind in the House of Commons. Indeed, one of the most surprising things of this whole surprising episode is the fact that this is a statement from the Canadian Minister of National Defence given in the Canadian House of Commons on a matter which affects Canadian defence policy, and it is headed "Statement being issued by the United States Department of Defence".
This leads us to suspect, Mr. Speaker, to say the least the adequacy of the consultation that has been going on in this matter, which is an unhappy reflection on the relationships between the two governments in a matter of such very great importance to Canada. So we ask the minister, why this snap decision on the part of the government made between Friday morning and Friday evening on a matter of such vital importance? If this decision-

May I ask the Leader of the Opposition to what decision he is referring as being made between the morning and the evening of last Friday?

Continental Air Defence Policy

The decision made is obviously embodied in the United States statement which the minister gave Friday evening at six o'clock. When we questioned him in the morning about a change in defence policy he said there was no such change and that press reports to that effect were speculative; I think that is the word he used. If a change was to be made in Canadian defence policy, why is it that the minister was not able to make a statement to that effect in the House of Commons on Friday morning, but had to wait until word presumably came from Washington that they were going to make a statement there and then read the United States statement in this House of Commons?

I wonder if I might answer that question right now. As was stated in the press itself, this was a leak from a meeting of a subcommittee of a committee on appropriations which was being held in camera. Does the Leader of the Opposition think I could hold up my head as an honourable member of this government and disclose a leak or disclose of information which I knew about? I was not going to confirm or otherwise a leak from a secret or in camera meeting.
If any such leak occurred, and perhaps it did-
I have said so. The Leader of the Opposition must accept my statement.

I accept the minister's statement that a leak occurred in congress because the government of the United States was telling a congressional committee about the changes that were going to take place in continental air defence. But no single member of this parliament who was not a member of the government had any indication at any time in the last month that the Canadian government was even considering such a fundamental change in defence policy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What change?

While discussion of defence policy was going on in Washington and while the minister now indicates that exchanges were going on between Canada and the United States in respect of it, we were unable to get one single word on defence policy from the minister at any time in the last two months. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, there was nothing to leak in this House of Commons because nothing was said either in public or in private.
That is why there was no leak.

That is the kind of consultation we have been having. I remember the Prime Minister, a couple of years ago in talking about the improvement in the relations between Canada and the United States, saying that everything was lovely now in the garden of Canadian-United States relations; he was tending the flower so carefully now that everything was fine. This statement does not indicate that this kind of consultation of which the Prime Minister was so proud a couple of years ago is really being very effective in so far as Canada is concerned, in the matter of national defence policy.
What has been the result of the United States decision, which presumably has been agreed to by the Canadian government? I now move on to the subject of the Bomarc B weapon itself, Mr. Speaker. The United States has presumably decided that the deterrent strength of the country-we are not subscribing to that deterrent strength except in an indirect way in Canada, it is the deterrent strength of the United States- should be increased. The minister's statement makes that matter quite clear, or rather the United States statement read by the minister makes that matter quite clear. It is to be increased, if necessary, at the expense of the strictly defence aspects of defence. I am not going to quarrel with that decision on the part of the United States authorities in which perhaps the Canadian authorities have concurred. It may well be that the best defence of peace at the present time is the strengthening of the deterrent. Perhaps the only defence of peace we have at the present time is the certainty on the part of those who might break the peace that, if they do so, they will be destroyed.
In any event, as the statement read by the minister makes quite clear, that is now to be the basis of continental defence policy in so far as it is determined by the United States, that a greater share of their resources is to be devoted to the deterrent strength of that country, and that the money and resources required for this increase of deterrent strength is to be taken from the project known as Bomarc B.
If anyone on the other side of the house thinks this does not represent a change in United States policy in respect of the Bomarc B, all they have to do is read the statement from the minister and the statements that are coming out of the United States at the present time. There is no doubt in the world that in this change the United States government is down-grading the Bomarc B. How otherwise can you explain a slash from $421 million for defence to $50 million? I know the minister has been saying-and indeed

it is quite correct-that funds are available from previous appropriations which will enable more than $50 million to be spent on this project. But the fact remains that in so far as the United States is concerned, the $421 million appropriated is to be reduced to $50 million. The down-grading of this weapon appears in practically every line of the statement read by the minister last Friday.
Yet to add to our confusion, and to add to the kind of anxiety that is being shown in the country, in practically every editorial I have read this morning which has commented on events over the weekend-I refer to the Globe and Mail, the Gazette and other papers; and in order to prove this confusion and uncertainty in people's minds, may I recall that yesterday, outside of this house and on a television program, the minister went to some pains to show that this did not represent any great change in the policy of the United States government in respect of this particular weapon.
I have not the text of what he said. I tried to get it, but I understand he was speaking merely from notes. However, I think the minister will agree that he said yesterday on the air-and this is in striking contrast to the impression created by his statement on Friday-that the change in the United States Bomarc program as the result of this statement made on Friday would not be very substantial, that there would still be 12 Bomarc squadrons left plus two Canadian squadrons, which would make 14 squadrons. If in fact that is the situation now, that is a very minor change. But that is certainly not what this particular statement says. How can the minister justify a statement of that kind, that we are still going to have 14 Bomarc squadrons in spite of the changes in Washington, including two Canadian Bomarc squadrons the missiles for which would be paid for by the United States?
Will the hon. gentleman permit a question?
Yes.

If these figures are correct, that there will be 12 Bomarc squadrons in the United States and two Bomarc squadrons in Canada, would the small reduction that is being made be understood by the minister as a proper one and not a major change of policy?

If that is in fact the situation, we have more cause than ever to criticize the minister for the statement he made last Friday.
Continental Air Defence Policy

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Leader of the Opposition is running away from the question.

I will come to the question in the next point, and it is a very easy question to answer. If that in fact is the situation, will the minister explain the reduction of $421 million to $50 million to be spent on these Bomarc squadrons? The minister himself on March 7, 1960 as reported at page 1789 of Hansard, had this to say when he told us we were losing our sense of proportion because we were worried about what was happening in the field of national defence, and especially in respect of this particular weapon which had been tried seven times and seven times found wanting.
So what?

"So what", says someone on
this side. How many times does it have to fail before this government will give up on it?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: May I ask a question?
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Did the Leader of the Opposition appreciate that the Bomarc A had 80 failures before it finally succeeded?

Of course I appreciate that.
I have been told that enough times in this house; and I have also been told that the Bomarc A was not adequate for the job we have to do, that we need the Bomarc B. If the Bomarc A was such a fine weapon and had so many successes after 80 failures, why do we not arm our forces with the Bomarc A instead of the Bomarc B? We are now discussing the Bomarc B, which the minister has said is to be the basic missile weapon for the Canadian air force, even though it has failed seven times in a row. These are just growing pains apparently, these failures.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Will the hon.
gentleman answer the Prime Minister's question?

When we discussed this
matter we were told that we were losing all sense of proportion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. Unless the hon.
member who has the floor wishes-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I just wished to
ask him to answer the Prime Minister's question.

I would be glad to. Here
is what the minister said with regard to

Continental Air Defence Policy this matter, as reported on page 1789 of Hansard for March 7:
I might mention that the United States, in this fiscal year, is spending $421.5 million for the development of Bomarc sites across this continent, of which there are 18 interlocking sites. Two of these will be constructed in Canada.
The minister told us on March 7 that the United States is going to spend $421.5 million on 18 Bomarc B sites, including two in Canada. He tells us now that the $421.5 million has been reduced to $50 million; and then he tells people of this country over the air that $50 million will do the work in respect of 14 stations, when he said on March 7 that $421 million would be required for 18 stations. Perhaps the minister can explain that; perhaps he will answer it now. Are there to be 14 Bomarc B stations constructed by the United States and Canada costing $421.5 million this year?
Mr. Speaker, that was the impression he had been giving us, and up until Friday last we had assumed that was quite correct and there was no change. Then suddenly this statement is issued by the United States which said, "we are going to cut this expenditure". Some of the people in the Boeing aircraft company have gone much further even than the statement in regard to the cut. But the minister having given that impression to the country, he tells us now there will be a great change in the whole Bomarc program. Indeed, he said outside the house on Friday that if the current development of the Bomarc did not succeed, it would be out completely. That is from a report in the Montreal Star. Then on Sunday he said that the changes are very minor, not substantial, and we will have 14 instead of presumably 18 Bomarc B squadrons.
Mr. Speaker, the minister then wonders why there is confusion and uncertainty in the country over our national defence policy. A Washington report of last Saturday quotes an official of the Boeing aircraft company as saying that the reduced funds for all these missiles made by the Boeing aircraft company will permit no major production at all, but will be used only to continue research.
From what is the hon. gentleman reading?
From a press statement from Washington attributing a report to a high official of the Boeing aircraft company.
What is the newspaper?
I have not got it before me-
Ah.

-but the Prime Minister
does not have to believe me if he does not


want to. I make this statement on my own responsibility as an hon. member, and that should be good enough for the Prime Minister. As a matter of fact it would not be very difficult for me to get the clipping, because there are a lot of others to the same effect.
The fact is that unless the minister can give us evidence to the contrary, this $50 million will probably serve the same purpose as the $50 million the Prime Minister talked so much about when the Arrow was scrapped. I am
pleased to see that the Minister of National Defence and the Leader of the Opposition are once again on friendly terms in the house, even though they are not entirely in agreement as to the policy which is being followed by the government.
The motion moved this afternoon by the Leader of the Opposition asks for the adjournment of the house-
-for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the lack of adequate consultation between Canada and the United States, as revealed in statements made by the Minister of National Defence on and since Friday last, on the basic change made by the government of the United States in continental air defence policy, together with the decision of the minister to continue unchanged Canadian expenditures on a weapon for which a drastic cut has been proposed in the United States defence budget.
I think there is substantial evidence to support the contention that there is a lack of adequate consultation between Canada and

Continental Air Defence Policy the United States. I think the minister himself, in his statement to the house on Friday last in reply to a series of questions, indicated clearly that there is inadequate consultation. As a matter of fact, from the minister's own statement it would seem clear that although he knew something was brewing in the United States, that some inquiry was being made and that some changes might well be made in defence policy, he had no idea that a sweeping change of the magnitude mentioned in the statement he made a few hours later was under contemplation. I say this because the Minister of National Defence had this to say in reply to the initial question put to him by the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer). The hon. gentleman said:
Mr. Speaker, Canada has been consistently consulted regarding a possible revision of the joint air defence plan which might be adopted in order that the development of defence and warning against ballistic missiles might be accelerated.
There are so many qualifications-so many "mights" and so many "possibly's"-in that statement by the minister that it seems to me he did not expect such sweeping changes to take place. The minister's defence, the minister's reply, is that he could not reveal to the house the discussions which were taking place because they were in camera. I would not ask the Minister of National Defence to reveal to the Canadian parliament matters which were before a United States committee in camera, but I do think the minister could have been more forthright with the Canadian parliament and public in the last few months by pointing out that there was every possibility of major changes being made in the defence policy of the United States and, as a result, in the defence arrangements between the two countries.
Instead, the people of Canada have been given no inkling that these sweeping changes might take place. They have been led to believe by the minister's statements that if reliance were placed on the Bomarc missile, the greatest defence possible would be achieved. I think it is disturbing that we should have been able to obtain fuller reports over the radio, a few hours before the questions were put to the minister, than were disclosed to this house; or that people in New York, for example, who read the New York Times should have been in a position to read a story in the issue of Friday, March 25, under a Washington date line of March 24, setting out very clearly the precise proposals which were made to the United States congress.
I repeat that what concerns me most is not the fact that the Canadian government did not disclose secret negotiations, but that it never took parliament or the Canadian people

into its confidence even to the point of saying that there were very serious matters under consideration in the United States in connection with this whole defence concept which might very soon lead to a drastic change in our own defence plans.
And also tell our potential enemies that.

Well, I suppose our potential enemies have access to the New York Times and probably learn some of the statements which are made on the radio from time to time, although it is impossible for a member of parliament to get from our Minister of National Defence a frank appraisal of the defence situation on this continent and the consultations on defence which are taking place.
For some time the C.C.F. party has questioned the effectiveness of the Bomarc B even at the operational stage as an adequate or worth-while object of expenditure for the defence of this country. Let me hasten to say that we are most anxious that in every respect our way of life-the democratic foundations of this nation-shall be given the fullest protection. But we think it is not protection, and it is not defence, to be spending vast sums of money on weapons which afford little if anything by way of protection. The Bomarc B is a weapon against manned bombers, as I understand it. I do not think there is any military expert here who does not believe that in the case of an all-out Soviet attack by say 1,000 manned bombers, 500 or at least a large proportion of the attacking force would succeed in getting through. Certainly enough would get through to wipe out our civilization as we know it. The protection of this country comes not from a potential number of potentially operative weapons that could wipe out perhaps only a minor percentage of attacking bombers equipped with atomic weapons; rather the protection of this continent comes from the availability of a deterrent, a counteroffensive being undertaken that would wipe out the nation foolish enough to make an attack on this continent.
That is the pith and substance of the United States statement that was read in this house. The United States have decided that there should be a tremendous reduction in their expenditures on the Bomarc, from $421 million to $50 million, in order to concentrate on the development of a deterrent, the ICBM's and IRBM's. We think this is the only military protection there can be for us and for the western world at this time, namely a mutual deterrent.

These are not ideas that are being advanced for the first time today. I made a "Nation's Business" broadcast on January 22 in which I had this to say:
The Bomarc missile on which Canada will spend hundreds of millions of dollars is already obsolete and a waste of the taxpayers' money. The Bomarc, even with nuclear warheads, would not shoot down enough Soviet planes in the event of an attack to prevent the total destruction of the country. In other words, enough Soviet planes would always get through in a single attack to wipe us all out. This shows that when even dealing with airbreathing aircraft, the Bomarc is absolutely a waste of money from beginning to end.
Canadian defence policy apparently remains unaltered in view of all the substantial changes. We feel that these expenditures are not adding to the defence of Canada. The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) at the beginning of this session placed on the order paper a resolution which outlined in some detail the attitude and policy of the C.C.F. with respect to general defence. We feel that recent developments have underlined the correctness of the position we took at that time.

Canada is not only a junior partner in the common defence of this continent but is not an effective partner, even in terms of adequate consultation. I think I should speak at this time because a number of points have been raised which must be cleared up otherwise they will give a very false impression to the people of this country. I have endeavoured to take down rough notes of what has been said. I cannot be quite certain that I have written word for word every point that has been raised.
The first part of this motion deals with the means of consultation that there are between Canada and the defence department of the United States. There are many means, and there is frequent consultation. I should like to run over the general means of consultation, and I want to try to give some idea of the amount of co-operation that there is between Canada and the United States. First of all, shortly after the change of government, this government established the NORAD organization. This was to ensure that there could be frequent consultation between those who are responsible for the defence of this continent. The defence of the North American continent is indivisible. You cannot develop a separate defence for Canada and a separate defence for the United States.
Experience over the last half century has shown that those countries which tried to stand alone were very quickly swallowed up by aggressors. It is only by taking cooperative action prior to the outbreak of war that you can ensure that there will be a proper combined defensive organization set up. I believe that the experience of the past 50 years has shown that had such a defensive agreement been reached in the earlier part

of this century, and had it been known that the commonwealth or the United States would enter world war I and world war II, it is quite possible there might not have been any such wars at all. Our fundamental policy, therefore, being that of a deterrent against war, we entered into this North American defence organization which is known as NORAD.
We have at NORAD not only the deputy commander but quite a large number of staff officers who are integrated into the command. If not at the moment, then recently, there has been a Canadian head of the operational division. They are in constant touch with the plans which are being projected for the defence of this North American continent. This organization was set up by this government and we have insurance, in that way, of consultation between the commanders, because the commander at NORAD is every bit as much a Canadian commander as he is a United States commander. He has visited Ottawa frequently and has laid his plans before our chiefs of staff who have had every opportunity to examine those plans and have sent back their comments on those plans. Those comments, to my knowledge, have resulted in modifications of the original plan. That is one level of consultation.
We also have at Washington a considerable staff of officers who are in daily contact with their opposite numbers in the Pentagon. Actually there are today some 60 Canadian officers of the army, the navy and the air force who are sitting in daily on various committees at the Pentagon and from the senior officer-who is Air Vice Marshal Hendrick -right down through that group of officers, they are in daily consultation. They keep the chiefs of staff here in Ottawa advised by letter, telegram and telephone. There is hardly a day but what the chiefs of staff are advised as to the plans which are formulated or which are being developed jointly by the Canadian and the United States officers for the defence of this continent.
Then again, a year or so ago, this government set up a committee of cabinet ministers to confer with their opposite numbers in the United States. The late Mr. Sidney Smith, then secretary of state for external affairs, was the first secretary of state for external affairs to attend a meeting of that committee which at that time was held in Paris. We now have the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), myself and the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. O'Hurley). The last meeting was held last fall at Camp David.

If there is any question at all about that meeting being a meeting of consultation, I should like to emphasize the fact that there was no long table at which we sat down with minutes and paper before us. However, we sat around in an informal group and we had the most intimate discussion on all defence matters. That meeting was attended by advisers. The chairman of the Canadian chiefs of staff committee, namely General Foulkes, was there as was General Twining, the chairman of the United States general staff, and Mr. Gates who was then assistant secretary of defence and now is secretary of defence in the United States. We were also represented by other officials than those of the Department of National Defence. The Department of External Affairs was represented there by its officials. Officials of the Department of Finance were there as were officials of the Department of Defence Production.
At that meeting one of the decisions arrived at was that there should be meetings of the committee of consultation which had not met for some long time previously. However, we thought that if we could revive this committee of consultation consisting of the senior officers of the various departments it could do a great deal of preliminary work prior to meetings of the ministers. A date has already been set early this summer for the next meeting of this committee of ministers. They are to come to Canada this time where there will be every opportunity again of having a thorough discussion of these defence matters at the very top level. It has been decided that there will be two meetings a year of the ministers in the two countries. I suggest that is top level consultation.
In connection with the particular matters to which reference has been made may I say that for weeks I have been familiar with some of the various proposals which were being advanced by the United States joint chiefs of staff, by their air force, turned over and discussed again with the commander at NORAD; and, because he is a Canadian commander as well as a United States commander, those recommendations advanced or the various proposed schemes which were being worked out were referred to us.
As recently as last Saturday week I was talking at some length to the secretary of defence for the United States, namely Mr. Gates, who called me-I did not call him- on the long distance telephone in order to explain to me in detail various proposals. He was leaving the next day in order to go to Germany and he said, "I want to get your views on these matters before I leave for Germany". That was last Saturday week.

I do not believe any hon. member would really have done that.
Following my remarks on Friday morning I was again in touch with Washington. I said that this information, some of it not entirely correct, had been published in Canadian papers and that I thought it was my duty to make a statement in this house if I possibly could in order to clear up the situation. Because I had stated before that it was a speculative story, and if Washington was going to make a statement I said I thought it should be made at the same time as any statement made in the House of Commons. The original statement was to be given out in Washington at 5.15 p.m. As there had not been time to get that statement and reproduce copies here, I asked for a postponement of that time of release in Washington until 5.45, at which time I rose in my
2510	HOUSE OF
Continental Air Defence Policy place here and asked for leave to revert to motions so that I could make that statement.
The statement I received, of course, was the statement the gist of which I had received some days before. I had one extra copy, and when I received a request from the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) I sent him the only spare copy I had so that he might have an opportunity to read it beforehand. As it had come across to me typewritten, it was headed: "Statement being issued by the United States department of defence". I had tried to accommodate the Leader of the Opposition, but now he is tearing his hair because the piece of paper I sent him over so hurriedly in order that he might have a chance to read it through beforehand happened to bear that heading.

On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, that is not what I was complaining about. What I was complaining about was that the statement which had been given to the press and also used in this house had a United States heading instead of a Canadian heading. There is your consultation.

I have described the origin of that statement and the events which took place between the morning session and the evening. Remember that this was a Friday afternoon, the last hour of which is normally devoted to private members' business. But I thought it was desirable that the house should be fully acquainted with all the proposals. If there had been time I could very well have put out a joint Canadian-United States statement, but it was a question of time and getting it out for the information of hon. members.
I feel I have disposed now of these suggestions that there is not adequate consultation between the two defence ministries. If I have not told hon. members of the House of Commons what these proposed plans were and how they were gradually being evolved, I have kept the members of the government informed in that respect, particularly the Prime Minister. There is no question about not being informed ahead of time or not being consulted. I have explained the various processes of consultation.
Now let me deal with this idea that a snap decision was made between nine and six o'clock last Friday that there should be a change. If I could produce the papers, which are all classified, showing how months ago the search to see how funds could be changed from the pure defence of the North American continent to that of increasing the power of retaliation, it would prove conclusively that no snap decision has been made.


This matter has been under consideration for months. I stood up in this house and explained two years ago how there was a general shift in emphasis coming gradually toward the missile rather than the bomber. But it was a gradual transfer. The fact that there were likely to be changes has repeatedly been stated. None of our defence plans can be rigid and fixed. There must be a large degree of flexibility, because not only are they dependent upon local conditions but they are also dependent upon the attitude of any possible aggressor. If different plans or inventions come to light which a possible enemy may have adopted, naturally you have to change your own defence plans in order to meet those changing threats.
Time and time again the Prime Minister and I have stood up in this house and referred to the changing threat, from bomber gradually towards missile. I am not going to take up a lot of time in making quotations. I have not had the opportunity to look them up, but I will just mention one. On January 18 of this year the Prime Minister of Canada spoke in this house, as reported on page 69 of Hansard, and he said this:
Defence policy cannot be certain. If it could be certain, and if we could determine today the course for the next three or four years, great savings might be made. If when the hon. gentleman was a member of the government-
The Prime Minister was there referring to statements made by the Leader of the Opposition.
-it could have been determined in 1945 or 1946 the changes that would take place in the intervening years, billions of dollars could have been saved in Canada on expenditures that had to be made for materials that are today obsolete. If we could anticipate what the U.S.S.R. would do, naturally we would be able to look into the future as to the course that should be followed with the same clarity that all of us can look into the past.
On the same day, in speaking to congress the President of the United States had this to say:
The last few years have witnessed what have been perhaps the most rapid advances in military technology in history. Some weapons systems have become obsolescent while still under development...
Thus, in the last few years a number of programs which looked very promising at the time their development was commenced have since been completely eliminated.
Those are two quotations which indicate that some time ago it was realized that changes must be made in defence policy and in the type of equipment being used by our defence forces.
These are fundamental changes which have taken place. We are in a period of transition which, I suggest, is unequalled at any time in history. I think it is almost a platitude to

say that. We are changing from the day of the manned bomber; now we are talking about missiles; and we have begun to talk about satellites being used for military purposes. That is a long, long way from the type of equipment which was used at the end of the last war.
References have been made to the future. There is no government in the world today which is more sincere in its quest for effective disarmament than the government of Canada. Canada is taking a leading part in the discussions which are now going on, but we would be wrong- we would not be living up to our responsibilities-if we were to anticipate the results of these disarmament conferences by taking action before an effective and enforcible system of disarmament is achieved. We must maintain, not so much our defence as our deterrent power. We base everything on the hope that we can deter an enemy from going to war. I have repeatedly said in recent weeks that there is no defence at the present time against the missile once it has been launched. Therefore we must do everything we can to prevent missiles being launched, and this means we must let the Russians, if they are our enemy, know that if they once start a war they will be met by such a tremendous counter-attack, such retaliation, that the loss to their own country would be so great that it would be suicide for them to attempt war.
The whole philosophy of our defence at the present time is that of a deterrent to war rather than of the actual defence of any particular country. I am not going to stand here and say we can shoot down every bomber that there is. I have heard statements made in this house in the past which were fantastic in the claims they made with regard to the number of bombers that could be shot down. I do not pretend for one moment that the defences we have can shoot down every bomber that might be sent against us. Mind you, the Russians have in their inventories in service today with their air force a large number of bombers, some of which are obsolete, some of which are more modern. None of them, to my knowledge, are supersonic as was claimed by the Leader of the Opposition. I do not know where the hon. gentleman got that information, but I have heard no analysis of the Soviet equipment which makes me believe that the Russians have supersonic bombers in operation today.

On that point raised by the minister, I got the information from a statement he made to the committee of estimates discussing defence two years ago last summer.

Continental Air Defence Policy
As far as I know the Russians have no supersonic bombers today. They may have tomorrow.
Oh, oh.

They are always changing. I do not laugh at that statement, though hon. members on the other side may. The Russians are changing and advancing in just the same way as we are. They have more advanced types of bombers than those which were in operation when the CF-100 was first made. I have made that statement before. It is quite possible, indeed, it is almost certain, that if war were to break out in the near future Russian bombers would be used.
I claim we have no protection against the missile today. The missile, once launched, cannot be shot down. Missiles will very likely be directed against the forces of retaliation which are, in the main, concentrated in the United States. However, it is more than likely that after the attack in the United States with missiles a bomber attack against the industrial cities would follow.
Nobody has told me that there will not be a war in the next three or four years. I do not think it is likely that there will be one. I do not think that the Soviet union is preparing for war against us today. Nevertheless, I am Minister of National Defence, and to a very large extent I am responsible for the defence of this country against any form of attack which may occur today, next year, or ten years from now, and while we make plans for ten years hence, I still have the responsibility, and the service chiefs still have the responsibility of meeting any possible attack today as best we can.
However, our funds are not unlimited and we would only be playing into the hands of an enemy if we set a burden upon the manpower and financial resources of our country sufficient to meet every possible form of attack. By doing so we should really be reducing the economy of our country to such a state as to be making ourselves susceptible to, may I say, psychological forms of attack. Thus, without overburdening the manpower and the financial resources of the country we have to provide the best form of defence that we can.
I have said, and I repeat it, that there is no defence against the missile once launched. We must therefore stress the power of retaliation. Canada does not play a very important part with respect to the power of retaliation. It has been said we are not in that league because of the enormous expenditure which is required to produce these modern weapons of retaliation. Perhaps I should mention a few of the costs involved. Some of the weapons which the United States started to

Continental Air Defence Policy develop and later had to abandon because of changing conditions included the Dart, an anti-tank guided missile on which some $10 million had been spent. After spending some $387 million, the United States navy abandoned the P6M, and the F8U3 was abandoned after the expenditure of some $136 million. The missile Regulus was abandoned after $120 million had been spent and other missiles which have been abandoned include the Rascal after an expenditure of $448 million and the Navaho, a missile on which there was an expenditure of $679.8 million.
To give hon. members some idea of the cost of some of these missiles of retaliation which are the only defence the west has at the present time-the power of retaliation-there is the Atlas and the Titan. Their development cost over $5 billion. Only a few of the Atlas are in operation. The cost of the Polaris in the fiscal year 1961 is expected to be $952 million. One nuclear carrier costs $471 million. That gives some indication as to why Canada cannot possibly enter that league where great sums of money have to be spent on the forces of retaliation.
What do we do? We are spending large sums of money on defence, part of which is spent on the defence of the North American continent. Part of the expenditure on defence of the continent is devoted to the Royal Canadian Navy so that with our surface ships and marine aircraft we can keep the hostile submarines away from our shores and prevent them launching missiles against our inland cities.
We spend considerable sums of money- millions-on the air defence of this continent in our warning systems which we provide, in part with the United States, as warning against the possibility of bomber attacks. We are looking into the future, working out at the present time means of assisting the United States in detecting the intercontinental ballistic missiles which might be launched against us. The main point of these warning systems is that the forces of retaliation, a number of which are still bombers in the strategic air command, can get off the ground in the few minutes that are available. If there was not that time to get off the ground they would be caught and destroyed on their air bases. Surely that money which is being spent on improving the warning systems is assistance to the only defence that we have at the present time, the power to make it clear to the enemy that it is not worth their while to attack.
We come now to the more immediate problem, the question of the change in the air defence plan. I have emphasized the point that retaliation is our one means of deterring

war, perhaps making it as difficult as can be for the enemy to attack. I am sure hon. members have read in the papers or heard comments about the so-called gap that exists between United States missile development and Russian missile development. At the present time the Russians may be a little bit ahead of the United States in their missile development but I think it is compensated by the fact that the United States has available for the defence of the west a variety of means of retaliation. Not only are there missiles presently in operation in United States-few in number, I will admit, but with others coming along in the next year or two-but there is a very large force of bombers which can travel from United States and deliver their bombs on the targets of every city in European and Asiatic Russia if Russia ever starts the attack. Also, to increase the diversity and flexibility of the powers of retaliation from the United States there are the United States submarines-again perhaps few in number but with more coming along *-which will have the potential of firing missiles. More and more submarines capable of carrying a Polaris will come into operation which will be able to go to any part of the world and from their unknown position in the ocean deliver their missiles against Russian targets.
In addition to that there are the medium range missiles of the Thor and Jupiter type stationed in the United Kingdom and planned for various European countries. And so, if the United States is a little behind Russia in the actual number of ballistic missiles they have, that is compensated for by the diversity of the United States weapons.
I see that you are on your feet, Mr. Speaker. I hope you are not going to stop me.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I hesitate to interrupt the hon. minister in the middle of a sentence, but unless the house gives indulgence I am obliged to advise the hon. gentleman that his time has expired.
Mr. Speaker, I think the minister should be allowed to continue.
Agreed.

Thank you. As I was saying, there may be a gap but that is partially compensated by the diversity of the United States means of retaliation. The United States realizes that it is essential that they speed up the production of their intercontinental ballistic missiles so as to close any gap that may exist. Even United States funds, however, are not unlimited. They have to draw from somewhere the money to

provide these very expensive weapons and so, because the threat from the bomber is decreasing, they have decided in consultation with Canada and the Department of National Defence that sacrifices must be made in the actual physical defence of this continent in order to make more funds available this year from purely defence to speeding up and increasing the power of retaliation.
The Bomarc program is considered an essential part of the defence plan of the North American continent so that they may deter bombers from coming over and so that some degree of defence can be given to the populated centres of the North American continent which are mainly concentrated in the east both in Canada and the United States. It so happens that the eastern approaches are the ones most likely to be followed up by Russian bombers if Russian bombers are used to follow up attacks of the missiles.
There had been a plan of some 18 Bomarc units distributed across the continent. Some of these stations-approximately four-have been eliminated. Those are ones which were not giving direct protection to the highly industrialized part of Canada. But the remaining stations, three of which are in operation, five of which are under construction in the United States at the present time, are distributed so that they can give protection to Canadian cities from Winnipeg to the Atlantic. There is more than one Canadian city today that will not benefit from the Bomarc plan when it is completed, and it is expected that this Bomarc plan will be completed, or that the last stations will come into operation, in 1963. They will cover every city from Winnipeg to the Atlantic, not our two Canadian ones. Our two Canadian Bomarcs, when established at North Bay and La Macaza, will give coverage from approximately Sault Ste. Marie to Quebec. Halifax is covered by Bomarc stations in Maine in exactly the same way as Winnipeg will be covered by Bomarc stations in the middle west.
That is the picture. There will be this chain of mutually supporting interlinked stations built to cover the Canadian air space for some 400 miles north of the border. The two Canadian stations are key links in that chain. I want to emphasize the fact that this is not an isolated defence; that these are not two lonely stations all by themselves. They are two important links in this chain of stations, and I cannot emphasize this too much because it does not seem to be realized by the general public.

Will the minister permit a question on this point? Is this chain of
Continental Air Defence Policy stations that he is talking about, the 12 or 14 in the United States, to be equipped with Bomarc A missiles or Bomarc B missiles?

Three are in operation today. Those are equipped with Bomarc A missiles. The Bomarc B missiles will be at other stations. I cannot tell at the moment the number of stations which are A's and the number designated for B's; but in the first instance it will probably be about 50-50. Then, if there is still a threat from the bomber, according to the original plans, the B would take over from the A station.
May I ask the minister this question. Is it contemplated that from its present appropriations the United States will equip those stations with Bomarc B missiles?

It is contemplated and there are funds available in the appropriation to equip a number of those stations. I am not saying all because three are already operative. The sum of $2,230 million has already been allocated by the United States for this program.

How much of that has been
spent?

As the Leader of the Opposition knows perfectly well, the funds do not go back to the general treasury once they have been voted. There are hundreds of millions of dollars still left in that appropriation for them to develop the program. It is quite wrong to think that $50 million is the only money available. There has been a reduction in order to make more money available for the powers of retaliation. There has been a reduction from $421 million, which was in the original plan drawn up a year ago, to $50 million; but the money which is allocated for the Canadian stations and for other stations in the United States not yet under construction is already voted and available to the United States air force for that particular purpose.

May I ask the minister this question, because it is a very important aspect of the matter, and we have heard nothing about this previously. There is enough money presumably available, from the minister's reply, for the United States to complete its present Bomarc B program?
It depends-do not smirk and smile like that-it depends entirely on what the Leader of the Opposition means by the present program.
There must be a program.

There is the present program which includes the whole 18 stations. There is a suggested change in that program not

Continental Air Defence Policy yet approved by congress. There is not enough money-if the amount is reduced to $50 million-to provide for all the original ones, but there is ample money to provide for the reduced: number. The reduced number is 14 units.
Some of which are A and some of which are B?
Some of which are A. At the present time there are three operational, and since there are no B's operational those three must be A's.
We are now getting our defence policy.

speechtext: The Leader of the Opposition has to have it explained.

There was an interruption and I have lost my trend of thought. I hope that has cleared up the situation. I repeat, up to June of 1960-and, remember, the United States fiscal year starts on July 1- $2,230 million has been allocated to the Bomarc program and Bomarc only; it has nothing to dp with SAGE; it has nothing to do with gap fillers. Let me make that quite clear. Do not get confused about other things as you have been confused about the costs of the Canadian Bomarc.
How much of that has been spent already?

I have not be actual figures. I tried during the debate to get the actual figures. All I can state at the moment is that there are hundreds of millions of dollars not yet spent; that is all they could tell me at the time. I should think that is adequate.
I think I have shown clearly that this is not a useless weapon. This is part of the essential defence of the North American continent. Of course, all weapons are useless perhaps, if they are not used in defence, unless you recognize the fact that they are useful in that they do deter the enemy from going to war. Withdraw those Bomarcs, ruin that chain of defence and then you have left the continent wide open and there would not be a deterrent to the Russian bombers which we know are in the Russian air force today. If we can maintain peace for the next five years, then you may say quite definitely that this has been a most useful weapon and that it has played a very prominent part in the power of retaliation, the power of the deterrent to deter the enemy from attacking this continent with bombers.
You have asked me about the effectiveness of the Bomarc B. Hon. members opposite, with one exception, have almost been rejoicing in the failures that there have been of this weapon.
Oh, oh.
They have given every indication that they were pleased that this weapon, in which I have said I have confidence, had again failed. It has failed seven times.
Why shouldn't we mention it, then?
It is not merely the mention of it, but it is the pleasure which has been shown on your faces when you have mentioned it.
Another form of closure.
Oh, oh.
We must not even talk about these things; cannot speak about anything.
