These tests of the Bomarc B have been carried out. Those who are connected with it, the officials who have watched these tests, the officials of the company, the officials of the department of defence of the United States, have repeatedly stated, and only as recently as today, that they have confidence in the ultimate success of this weapon. When you come to think of it, you are trying to devise a weapon which has to hit another very small target which is travelling well over 500 miles an hour and at a distance of 400 miles away. That is not an easy thing for anybody to develop.
This Bomarc B is based on the same principle as the Bomarc A. The Bomarc A, within the limits of its range, has proved to be a successful weapon.
Two hundred miles.

This is doubling that range, but the basis is the same. I have confidence that this weapon will be developed, based upon the information and the statements that I have received. I feel that we should go on with our small share in the preparation for receiving these weapons. The instruments of the Bomarc B's, with their launching pads, when placed at our disposal, will have cost the United States and Canada somewhere in the neighbourhood of $91 million. We are contributing somewhere about $15 million in order to provide the housing and structures for these weapons. Some of the equipment has already been ordered. At the present time one of the sites is being cleared of the brush and the approach road is under construction. It is suggested that we should cancel that because some members opposite have lost faith in this weapon. I have not lost faith in the Bomarc B. I think we

should continue with the construction work. We are expecting to hear that further tests have been carried' out in the not too distant future. But the principle is sound and the United States have confidence in it.
I say that I welcome the motion which has called for the adjournment of the house because I have had an opportunity, for the first time, to show what our defence policy is. I have had an opportunity of replying to a number of incorrect statements which have been made by hon. members opposite giving a false impression to the people of this country. I have given hon. members information. I have held nothing back. I think any reasonable person can see that we have had every opportunity of consulting with our allies; that they have listened to our recommendations in many cases. We are constantly in touch with them, and I think I have shown clearly that the Bomarc is an essential weapon in our mutual efforts to deter the outbreak of war. We are going to stand by the agreement we have made with our allies. We have entered into an agreement for the development of these Bomarc stations, and we are not going to scrap that sacred agreement with our allies and give up just because somebody says there is a possibility that the Bomarc B may not be successful.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the house has listened with great interest to the speech of the honourable and gallant gentleman, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes). This is the 28th day of March and today marks the first statement that the Minister of National Defence has made in this house since the opening of this session, except for replies he has made to the questions which have been asked him from time to time. If the action taken by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) today serves no other purpose, it will serve the constructive purpose of having encouraged the Minister of National Defence to make at least one report this session on some aspects of defence policy.
It must not be forgotten that the minister with an associate minister is the head of a department that is responsible for a larger expenditure of public money than any other department of government. It is, perhaps, for the minister at some other time to explain why he has only now taken advantage of the opportunity, in the light of the importance of national defence both in terms of international application and of the national budget, to explain to the house some of the matters that he regards as vital to the security of the nation and to the unity of Canada's associated states in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.
Continental Air Defence Policy
It is amazing, however, to think that the minister should have used this opportunity of debate to say what the Leader of the Opposition had been denied the opportunity of saying in laying the foundation for his motion. How desirable it would have been if a defence committee had been set up along the lines suggested by him in which it would have been possible for members representing the various parties of this house to explore problems that are in the public mind but which, at this time, remain unanswered.
Order, order.

The Minister of National Defence has just finished a speech three quarters of which was devoted to defence policy. That opportunity was denied the Leader of the Opposition and pursuant to the policy of closure being followed by the government I am now being called upon not to make any comments on the remarks made by the Minister of National Defence. The Minister of National Defence discussed the particular issue only in the first ten minutes of his speech and in the last 15 minutes. The body of his speech had to do with defence policy which the Leader of the Opposition was not permitted to discuss.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. May I remind the hon. member for Essex East that if he had a point of order to raise and wished to object to the course followed by the Minister of National Defence, the time to do it was when he was transgressing.

I am not raising a point of order, Mr. Speaker. The point of order is being raised by hon. gentlemen who now want to deny to the opposition a right which the opposition did not deny to the Minister of National Defence.
Oh, oh.
I know the Prime Minister does not like this. He was the one who objected to what the Leader of the Opposition said.
Mr. Speaker, I particularly enjoy hearing the hon. gentleman discuss defence and I want him to have the opportunity of touching those peaks he normally touches when he knows little about a subject.

Once again, Mr. Speaker, we have the Prime Minister of this country upholding the great dignity of his office by making observations which, under our tradition, normally would be made only by one who sat in the last seat in the last row. The Prime Minister, of course, has such a high regard for the exposition of all the facts that it pleases him now and then to

Continental Air Defence Policy descend from his high office and to make such constructive observations as the one with which he has now delighted his followers. That procedure, of course, makes the Prime Minister a great parliamentarian.
I am sure the Minister of National Defence will regret having said that we on this side of the house rejoice in the failure of the Bomarc. That is a statement which I am sure the Minister of National Defence, on reflection, will want to withdraw. He knows perfectly well that it is the duty of an opposition to expose the weaknesses of the administration as it sees them. He knows that it is the duty of the opposition to discuss matters which it believes require attention by the administration. I should have thought that the hon. and gallant gentleman would welcome the opportunity to have this particular debate and that, while he might not agree with what hon. gentlemen in the opposition said, he might at least have attributed to them the sincerity of purpose which he expects-and rightly so-and which every hon. member in this house attributes to him. However, I let the statement of the Minister of National Defence speak for itself.
We are not rejoicing at these failures. We are sharing with the people of Canada generally at this time concern and disquietude over this particular matter and particularly over the conduct of national defence by the hon. gentleman and his colleagues who comprise the present government of Canada. That concern is reflected not only in the attitude of the party on whose behalf I am speaking at the moment but is reflected elsewhere in the nation.
In his attitude at the outset of today's deliberations the Prime Minister revealed the concern which he recognized is felt not only by members of this house but by people throughout the country generally because he did not give the Leader of the Opposition time to finish his argument but said, "We accept at once your proposal to discuss this particular matter of the Bomarc''. The reason the Prime Minister did so was that, good politician that he is, he recognized the fact that all over this country since Friday last there has arisen a question mark about this government's defence policy. That is the reason why the Prime Minister readily accepted the suggestion that debate on the matter now under discussion should be provided for under the procedure of moving the adjournment of the house.
Addressing himself to the question of consultation, which is one of the main arguments adduced by those of us in this party against the government at this time, the Minister of National Defence outlined the whole

mechanism of consultation which theoretically exists between the United States and Canada in matters of military affairs. No one denies that this set-up on paper presents an extremely complete picture. But the question at issue is whether or not, in this instance, the processes of consultation were operative; whether or not in the particular instance- altogether apart from the occasions or the instruments for consultation-they were in fact used; whether or not in fact the minister really was informed of the important events that were taking place in the United States.
As an example of the consultation that exists, the minister stated that he knew what was the total amount of moneys originally voted by the United States for this Bomarc program. Yet when asked by the Leader of the Opposition what was the total expenditure made to date out of the moneys voted the Minister of National Defence was not able to give a definite reply. If the consultation with the United States is as efficient as the Minister of National Defence says it is, surely it would not have taken very long for the Minister of National Defence, in preparing his material for today, to have ascertained from the United States how much money has already been spent out of the moneys voted in the United States for the Bomarc program. We would then be in a position to determine whether or not the argument made by the Minister of National Defence with regard to the future use of the Bomarc was deserving of the validity suggested by the Minister of National Defence.
I refer the house to a statement made by the Prime Minister when he spoke on February 20, 1959 in this house. That was on the occasion of the abandonment of the CF-105. As reported at page 1222 of Hansard of that year the Prime Minister stated as follows:
Having regard to the information and advice we have received, however, there is no other feasible or justifiable course open to us. We must not abdicate our responsibility to assure that the huge sums which it is our duty to ask parliament to provide for defence are being expended in the most effective way to achieve that purpose.
Those were wise words.
What page was that?

Page 1222. Those were words which the Prime Minister and the members of the government ought to apply to the present situation, namely:
We must not abdicate our responsibility to assure that the huge sums which it is our duty to ask parliament to provide for defence are being expended in the most effective way to achieve that purpose.
Whether or not one accepts the argument made by the Minister of National Defence,

no one will deny that as a result of the incidents on Friday last a prima facie case at least was established for questioning whether or not, in the particular context, public moneys were being properly used for the purpose intended.
In the same debate, as reported at page 1224 of Hansard of that year, the Leader of the Opposition stated as follows:
Surely if we are going to make this change from an interceptor developed and built in Canada to a missile developed and built in the United States, then we must be confident in our own minds-all of us who have an obligation in parliament in this matter-that this change is going to increase our lefence capacity.
In the light of the events which now confront us, how wise these words of the Leader of the Opposition were.
The principle which the Prime Minister has enunciated in his statement and which should guide not only Canadian but United States policy in this matter is the principle of the pooling of our resources continentally and on an Atlantic basis for collective defence. Surely that does not mean that Canada is to be asked to take part in collective continental defence in so far as planning and operation are concerned but not in so far as the development of resources and industrial capacity are concerned.
The important part of the statement of the Leader of the Opposition is that we have an obligation to make sure that this change is going to increase our defensive capacity.
Now, do events as they were unfolded on Friday and as told to us today by the Minister of National Defence meet the requirements laid down in these remarks of a year ago by the Leader of the Opposition? It is clear, Mr. Speaker, whether the minister agrees or not, that from the events of Friday last there is every justification for questioning the consultation that has prevailed between the United States and Canada in this matter. All we have to do is to review the incidents of Friday last in order to see how justified this statement is and how warranted are the fears of journalists in our newspapers who have expressed editorial opinion, as well as the remarks of commentators through other instruments of dissemination of opinion. At a time when, as the minister says, the intercontinental ballistic missile has provided many transformations in the defence policies of the countries concerned it would have been very helpful if the government had accepted the proposal for the setting up of such a committee so that the minister could have given the kind of statement he has made today and proper precautions for security could have been taken in the circumstances when necessary. It would be worth while for us to know in what particular areas of our own national defence these reductions could, consistent with security, take place.

He ought to have been prepared for that event. They ought to have had an agreed statement worked out beforehand and an agreed technique in case there was a leak, because there always are leaks. Was he in honour bound not to tell us that in this joint program in which we are supposed to be equal partners the United States government was proposing great changes to their congress but this parliament was not to be told anything about it? If the minister had any sense of his obligations to this parliament and to the people of this country he would have said, "This is intolerable; I cannot agree to it; if you are going to change this policy I insist on being able to tell the people of my country and to tell my parliament". Then even more extraordinary than that, it seems to me, was what the Prime Minister said to us this afternoon. He said the Leader of the Opposition had no business making the kind of motion he made. Why? Because the minister had gone on television and explained everything on television.
Oh, oh.

This is a new conception of the rights of parliament from the great exponent, the great advocate, the man who is going to restore the rights of parliament. What do we get? We get the unemployment policy announced by the Prime Minister on television within two hours of the time when the debate ends. We get defence policy announced on television on a Sunday. That is a new conception of parliament. That is the restoration of the rights of parliament which the hon. gentleman promised the people in this country in 1957 and 1958.
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that regardless of the merit of this question-and about the merits I do not pretend to be an expert at all and I am not going to speak about them-what I am saying is that in so far as the parliament of Canada is concerned, every right we have is being trampled in the dust. There is no better example of it than the example we had over this Bomarc question. Moreover, I say that it is intolerable to have our policy dictated to us over the telephone, to have the extraordinary situation we had on Friday morning where the minister speaks of speculation and rumour and then comes in at a quarter to six and says, "I have now orders from Washington; here they are; it is too late to debate them but here they are". Then there is such a commotion in the press over the week end that the Minister of National Defence gives an entirely different explanation over television and because that is done the Prime Minister says we have no right to raise the question in parliament.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: He did not say that at all and the hon. member knows it.

The hon. gentleman can look at the Prime Minister's words. The Prime Minister said that the Leader of the Opposition should not have brought in this motion because he knew the facts already.
Mr. Pallet!: Read his statement.
Continental Air Defence Policy

The hon. member for Peel, (Mr. Pallett), who never gets the point until it is repeated about three times, may look at the words of the Prime Minister if he wishes to do so and perhaps he will see that after all I am right and he is wrong.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: The hon. gentleman had better have a look at the speech tomorrow and see for himself what was said.
What is the point?

Someone says "What is the point?" The point is that we in this parliament are entitled, as soon as the United States congress gets it, to have a proper explanation of the joint policies of the two countries, if indeed they are joint policies. But nothing could be clearer to anybody who reads the editorial writers in papers like the Montreal Gazette and the Globe and Mail, which papers are not notoriously friendly to us but were once friendly to hon. gentlemen opposite-that they cannot find out anything about this matter except what they read in their news columns, it is not surprising that the rest of the Canadian people are puzzled. It also seems to me that that puzzlement, that confusion, that concern, that anxiety has not been assuaged at all by the explanation given by the Minister of National Defence. As for the purely political intervention of the Prime Minister, of course it did nothing to restore the dignity of parliament.
May I ask the hon. gentleman the question I wanted him to answer? Does the hon. gentleman know that the committee on appropriations has not yet reported to congress?

I am glad the minister asked me that question because that is one of the points I wanted to make. This afternoon the minister said-I have a note of it here-said something about it being flexible; yes, he said it was not a fixed plan. Those were his exact words. It is beyond my comprehension what the minister means by that statement. When the defence department of the United States goes to congress and says-
They have not gone yet. That is the point.

Perhaps the minister would allow me to reply. I am replying to his question. When they go and tell congress, "The defence department are suggesting that you cut this from $420 million to $50 million", does the minister really think that congress is going to force more money on them?
Quite possibly.

If it is, let me ask the minister this. Does that mean that congress, not

Continental Air Defence Policy even the United States defence department but congress, is making our defence policy, because that is what the minister is saying? In other words, the minister says that a policy put forward by the defence department is of no particular validity but that the congress of the United States from now on will make the defence policy of Canada. I do not think many Canadians are going to regard that as the end of subservience.
I wonder whether the hon. gentleman would answer a question for me?
Surely.
Would he tell the house how much of this reduction, about which he has made such a great thing, is coming out of the Canadian treasury?
I said that I would answer the hon. gentleman's question, but perhaps I did him too much credit. I thought the question would be intelligible and capable of an answer.
Just answer the question and do not make statements concerning my intelligence.

I quite frankly confess that I did not understand the hon. gentleman's question but if it means what I think it means, that the reduction in the American appropriation affects the treasury of Canada, the answer is apparently not, but I think it should.

Mr. Speaker, I am a little surprised, although not too much, that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) has made a political attack on the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) when he is unavoidably absent. This is becoming somewhat of a habit as far as he is concerned. The Prime Minister has a lot of business to attend to and the hon. member probably expects him to be absent when he speaks because many of his speeches are in a political vein.
In his opening remarks the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate made one statement that I thought was very intelligent. He said that he did not know anything about the Bomarc and therefore he was not going to talk about it. That was one of his more intelligent statements.
What was the other one?

The hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) talked about limbs being cut off. When the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes) wielded the axe I am sure that hon. members opposite were the ones who were sitting on the limb. The members


of the opposition seem to be rather confused about policy generally in respect of defence. They have no constructive criticisms to offer. However, I fear that many of their remarks are accepted in all good faith by the Canadian people and there is serious objection to this, particularly in a debate concerning the Bomarc.
The opposition brought up the matter of consultation and the minister quite openly gave the reasons for the consultations and said that there definitely had been consultations. When the hon. member for Essex East was talking about the leak of information or where the information emanated from he was kind enough to point out to the Minister of National Defence how such a situation could be handled. It was very nice of him, an exminister now in the opposition, to do that since he probably has a great deal of experience in offering advice but I would not think with regard to defence policy particularly.
I do not know about consultations with Washington but with respect to NORAD but I do have some knowledge about the organization. I have friends who have served in it and have now come back to Canada. One thing they are worried about is the fact that, instigated by the opposition, there has been a great deal of talk in the House of Commons and throughout the country to the effect that Canada is losing its sovereignty to the United States. They say that the Americans connected with NORAD have become supersensitive on this point and that not only do they consult on all matters but that they also lean over backwards to accept the advice of Canadian defence personnel assigned to NORAD. Yet, financially speaking, our share of the operation is very small although our voice is very loud. This is something that the people of Canada do not know. From the speeches made by members of the opposition both in the house and outside the people of Canada have been led to expect a great deal less.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate said that we had shown our abject subservience to the Americans with regard to the Bomarc. The minister explained how the leak occurred. The announcement was made by Washington at five p.m. and the minister made the announcement later. Does the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate think that the parliament and people of Canada should have been given this information before the people of the United States?
Would the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You would not allow one.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
You would not allow
one.
The hon. gentleman has done me the courtesy.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Give him the same courtesy.
I was going to ask the hon. member whether he does not think that we in this parliament are entitled to the information as soon as it is given to a committee of the United States congress?

Not as soon as it is given to a committee or subcommittee of the United States congress, especially when it is sitting in camera. The hon. member expects that we should have the information before the United States congress gets it.
Not before; at the same time.

That is absolutely ridiculous. Of course, the opposition wants much of this confidential information made known to the Canadian people before the people of the United States get it. I think he is probably right that there should be a joint announcement but in this case in was almost impossible to do so because of the unfortunate leak that occurred. It was really a joint announcement in that the Minister of National Defence could not make the announcement before a quarter to six because of the time lag.
With regard to the Bomarc missile, I hope the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) will go over Hansard very carefully and try to correct the impression he has given the Canadian people that the Bomarc missile is of no use and that nothing is of any use against missiles. No one has claimed that the Bomarc is an anti-missile missile.
Of course not.

The Leader of the Opposition left the impression that the Bomarc was a useless anti-missile missile. It was never claimed to be an anti-missile weapon at all.
The minister explained very carefully to the rather confused opposition about the Russian bombers and their increasing activity over the past two years. It is quite obvious to our observers that the Russian bombers are doing a great deal of training. Despite the fact that there is a gap in continental ballistic missiles, we still have the danger of the Russian bombers. We have in our armament a fairly good interceptor but, as the minister explained, we cannot estimate at what point the U.S.S.R. may be in possession of a supersonic bomber, and neither can the opposition unless they get a leak from the U.S.S.R. as well, and
Continental Air Defence Policy that might be possible. In these circumstances we are obliged to have some deterrent during the period of time which is available to us, and that will probably have to be the Bomarc ground-to-air missile.
There has been no change in our policy or in United States policy as far as the Bomarc is concerned. The opposition has made great play with regard to the reduction in expenditure from $421 million to $50 million. Though the minister explained the situation very carefully, his words did not seem to have reached or penetrated the minds of the opposition. The fact of the matter is that they have every confidence in this armament. Our policy, and everyone has known it for years, is defensive, and for this reason we do not take any large share in such a field as the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) referred to, perhaps inadvertently, when he stated that we should become full partners with the United States with respect to mutual deterrence.
I did not say that at all.

You had better read your Hansard. I listened very carefully to the hon. member and he said "mutual deterrence". That is beyond our means. That has been explained time and time again, and I am sure the hon. member for Assiniboia will make a proper correction. In the time gap of which I have spoken we shall still be in danger from Russia bombers. We must, therefore, be in possession of this line of defence, the 14 Bomarc units. If we drop the development of these units because of the anxieties felt by the opposition the idea would wrongly be raised in the minds of the Canadian people that we do not know what they are doing, but that the opposition does; that we are no longer capable of continuing to lead the country.
I should like to see any policy other than that advocated by the hon. member for Assiniboia who tried to speak on defence on television the other night, suggesting that no matter how much the government might go into the red we should give more money away to countries abroad.
As to the figure of $125 million, I am sure it was some sort of a mistake which arose in caucus between the two opposition groups. I remember that at one time, as announced in the press by one member of the C.C.F., it was stated that it was going to cost Canada $300 million. So the figure depends merely on how receptive the political audience is, and how many people are likely to question the figures. I do not know how often this matter has to be explained to the opposition. Perhaps in the defence committee the minister could take

Continental Air Defence Policy a blackboard and draw it and print it out in simple words. The opposition could be given copies, and then they might understand.
The minister has confidence in the Bomarc B. I have been told that the Bomarc A was tested 80 times, 82 times, in fact, before it finally became operational. There is no doubt, in my mind at least, that when there was this nonsense in the press that the Bomarc had failed it was repeated by the opposition with a great deal of relish, if not with rancour. Let us face this. The failings discovered by the research experts, despite Mr. York's remarks- he is only one of the defence experts concerned-are small failings which we are sure can soon be fixed, and this anti-aircraft missile will soon be operational.
My main worry about all this is how the Canadian people are going to take it. By their criticism and by the attitude they have taken the opposition are doing, I believe, unlimited harm. Most people do not go into these questions, except to read the headlines in the newspapers. They do not read the technical announcements which are made. A feeling of panic hits them, and they feel the situation is due to the weakness of government policy when, in fact, this is the first time we have had a policy of any fixed type for many years. If it is said that we have not done anything in the field of defence policy, I should like to remind the house of one thing, though it is probably not pertinent to this motion: What about civil defence? That, at least is receiving attention.
Oh.

There was a certain amount of freedom allowed to the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin). He did everything but tell us about the election in 1957.
I believe that in this to-do about the Bomarc bases we must face the fact that they are all part of a defensive line. If we abandon this project, the whole line is cracked. The United States would be forced to abandon it too, because it is the centre of the line, the part most important for ourselves and the United States. Unless we do our share we might just as well abrogate any agreements we have with the United States, including NORAD.

I suppose I, also, shall be condemned by hon. members on the government side because I have the temerity to say a few words about the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) when he is not here. However, I am afraid that if we have to wait until he is here before we can say anything which involves him, we shall need to keep silent for a great deal of the time we spend in this house. This is not a criticism of the Prime Minister, because I know


he is a busy man, but it is a criticism of government supporters who are so touchy that if anyone says anything about the Prime Minister in his absence then, right away, we hear this nonsense: you would not say that if he were here, and so on.
Today, when the Prime Minister rose and so eagerly accepted the challenge of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) to debate this matter of the Bomarc, I am sure we were all hopeful that at last we would get a little common sense out of this very senseless defence program we have been trying to examine for the last number of months. But I am afraid the Canadian people will be just as disappointed as I was.
I remember occasions when the Prime Minister took three hours in which to say nothing in this house, but today he succeeded in doing so in just ten minutes. In the four sessions of parliament that I have attended I never heard him say nothing so convincingly as he said nothing today. The defence he offered for the actions of this government over the past week fell flat on its face. The greatest head of steam he could work up was when he said categorically that Canada and the United States were two equals joined together. I said in this house last week that the only link joining us with the United States is the link joining the tail to the kite, and it is quite apparent that there is no communication line in that link.
The first paragraph of the interesting lead editorial in this morning's Montreal Gazette reads as follows:
The issue of the Bomarc B has produced almost complete confusion among the Canadian people. Rarely, in matters of defence, has the want of understanding between the government and the people become so wide. The practice of not taking the people fully and frankly into its confidence has left the government in a position where few Canadians understand what it is trying to do, or why it is trying to do it.
If the Prime Minister's speech today was designed to restore the confidence of the Canadian people in the defence policy of this government I would say his attempt was as big a failure as the Bomarc missile.
The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes) also attempted to put up a defence today and I must confess I felt rather sorry for him although I felt even sorrier for the Canadian people. He was faced with an unhappy situation today and I might have skipped him altogether in my remarks. I listened to him carefully and his position seemed to me to be as hopeless as it was last Friday when he expressed his abiding confidence in the Bomarc B. I think we should rename it the BB because in terms of defence today it is just about as useful as a BB

gun. Perhaps it will fly some day but as a defence weapon I think it is useless and fail to see how the minister can retain confidence in it. If it ever works, it is not even scheduled to become effective until 1964 which is four years from now. If we look at the happenings of the last three years it is no wonder that the Canadian people are confused at trying to find any sense in the present government's defence policy.
In the last two and a half years what have we seen? The missile-carrying Mark VI was scrapped because we had the Arrow. The Arrow was then scrapped because we had the Bomarc and now we see the Bomarc scrapped as well. I know that hon. gentlemen opposite will say it is not scrapped and that the sum of $50 million remains in the United States kitty for this project but I recall to the attention of hon. members opposite that we still had $40 million in the kitty when the Arrow was scrapped which was just enough to sweep out the empty shell where the Arrow used to be produced and the $50 million we have in the fund today would just about dust off the sites that have been abandoned.
The Minister of National Defence today failed to answer any questions to satisfy the Canadian people or ease the minds of the opposition. I will list just a few. I wish someone on the government side would explain why we have been given different figures representing the cost of these missile bases under the Bomarc program. We were first told that the United States was going to spend $72 million on these two sites in Canada and that Canada would contribute an additional $15 million, making a total of $87 million or a cost of $43.5 million for each site. Then we had an announcement by the minister on March 7 that there were to be 18 bases in the Bomarc line at a cost of $23.5 million each. Now he says the program has not been abandoned but just revised slightly. On March 25 we were told that there would be 14 bases at a cost of $3.5 million each. Is it any wonder that there is confusion in the minds of the Canadian people?
I have been searching for some reason for the adamant stand of the Minister of National Defence and his government with respect to this project. I finally found a reason today which perhaps makes some sense. It is contained in an article by Robert Duffy which appeared in today's Globe and Mail. This is the first indication I have had of a reason why the government adheres so rigidly to the program which has been scrapped by the United States. The article states in part:
Even the most cynical person here would not suggest that the government's undying loyalty to
Continental Air Defence Policy the Bomarc firework could be decided by electoral considerations. Nobody, however, has noted any tendency in the government to deal urgently with the question of whether or not the program should be revised.
The article deals, of course, with an event which may occur at the site of one of the two proposed bases in Canada, the one at Mont Laurier which is in the centre of a riding where there may be a by-election in the near future.
We have heard the government severely and justifiably criticized by the official opposition in respect to its defence program but the Liberal party has advanced no alternative. We therefore have had an indication of the similar problem we would be facing if the Liberals were in office today instead of the Conservatives.
I wish to read a paragraph from an article by Arthur Blakely, which appeared in the Montreal Gazette today and which reads in part as follows:
If, however, the Liberals have devised any genuine alternative to existing policies, they have kept it under wraps. They are much more cautious than the C.C.F.'ers about a unilateral program of disarmament. And they have had some difficulty in devising an acceptable alternative to an arms policy which is at least partially of their own making.
It is fine to criticize the government but it is not enough to do so. You should offer some kind of alternative.
I am pleased to see that the United States government has accepted the view this group has been advocating, that the only possible defence is a deterrent rather than just a straight so-called defence. The Prime Minister, the Minister of National Defence and hon. member for Portage-Neepawa (Mr. Fairfield) have said that a deterrent is beyond the means of this country and that may be so, but if it is true let us face up to the fact. A deterrent is the only defence we have in sight today.
What is the sense of going ahead blindly and spending millions of dollars when all we are doing is going through the motions of defence without ever having one bit of defence for the people of this country? The government seems to think that as long as we spend money we are defended. I say, Mr. Speaker, this is not a good enough answer for the people of this country today.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make one or two brief comments concerning the remarks of one or two hon. gentlemen who have preceded me and perhaps to say a word, not to enlighten them because at this stage they refuse to be enlightened by the Minister of National Defence, (Mr. Pearkes) or anyone else, but

Continental Air Defence Policy rather to make one or two corrections in the comments they have made. When you reach an impasse in a debate, when the opposition in effect say to you, "We have made up our minds; don't confuse us with the facts", the debate merely comes to a dead stop.
We have seen an interesting performance tonight, Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The same is true of the government occasionally.

As an example, we have seen the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), obviously ill-prepared, coming in here and giving us a lecture on air defence with little regard for the facts. We have seen the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), with his usual wind and fury, produce something less than his usual mouse. His chief concern apparently is that the statement read by the minister was on a United States letterhead rather than a Canadian letterhead. This was the whole point of his argument. My friend, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickers-gill), showed his usual lack of intestinal fortitude, which the services generally call guts, in making an attack on the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), something that he would not have done under any other circumstances.

Mr. Speaker, I am rising on a question of personal privilege. The hon. gentleman has suggested that I said things in the house this evening that I would not have said if the Prime Minister had been here.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: That is right.

The hon. gentleman knows perfectly well that that statement is completely untrue, and that 1 have said much harsher things about the Prime Minister when he was here. I might add, sir, that it is not my fault that the Prime Minister is not here.

I hardly think that is a question of personal privilege. I do not think it is going to be the most important factor in the debate. I merely make a comment on it because it has become rather consistent practise of the hon. member.
I wish to try to express in as simple a form as one can where the Bomarc fits into the defence system which as it is integrated and is not a single weapon, in our defence; not something on which we are entirely dependent for the continental defence of North America, but rather a component and which is in its early stages of experimentation, something which no one has denied.
(Mr. Smith (Calgary South).]
Before we examine this weapon let us remind ourselves, as the opposition, and in particular the Leader of the Opposition, failed to do, that when one talks about defence one must make some reference to all of the aspects which make up the total defence of this continent. We get the impression-and it is obviously one intentionally left by the opposition-that because this weapon has not been successful, or because the Canadian government rejected the Arrow, Canada is left completely undefended. Nothing is further from the facts and no one knows it better than the Leader of the Opposition.
I think it is safe to say that when this government, through its negotiations with the United States, introduced the defence alliance which we know as NORAD, it was the first step in continental defence that has made some sense in modern defence planning. It was quite obvious that a nation with a defence budget of $1,700 million and a population of 16 million people is not going to be able to give comprehensive continental defence either to itself or to its allies to the south. I have never been able to understand yet whether the opposition support the principle of NORAD or not, because they continually talk out of both sides of their mouths on this and other subjects.
NORAD, then, is a principle of defence upon which Canada must rely to a very large extent. I ask the Leader of the Opposition and his associates whether or not they support this principle? Second, I ask them whether or not they believe that our contribution is in any way subservient to that of the United States? It has already been clearly indicated that in Air Marshal Slemon, the deputy commander, we have the second most senior officer in the air force. In a Canadian air vice marshal we have the chief of operations. The fact is well-known, then, in this house and certainly to the Canadian people, that Canada, in relation to its contribution to all of the defence of the continent, has a far greater say in the continental defence of North America than the United States in proportion to the dollars that are put up for it.
I hope the day will come when we do not insist on dealing with questions of sovereignty in relation to defence which in effect are not questions of sovereignty at all but are introduced purely with a political motivation in order to confuse or distress the Canadian people by suggesting to them that they are going to lose their birthright. The fact of the matter is we share with the United States in the defence of the free world to a far greater extent than any other country. When we think of a budget of $1.7 million and some 16J million people, we see the picture in its proper perspective.

Let us look at Bomarc and this cost of $15 million and relate it to an integrated system which involves three large radar chains. To the sum of $15 million must be added two groups of separate squadrons of air defence; to the $15 million must be added a complete partner which has not only the use of the deterrent through the strategic air command, but defence squadrons of Europe and, of course, of the United States; the $15 million involves an over-all pattern of defence. This is the subject matter of the debate. I suggest that the $15 million item should be brought into perspective with our own defence expenditures, $15 million in a budget of $1,700 million.
The Leader of the Opposition moved the adjournment of the debate to express a complete lack of confidence, as he said, in the defence policy, because of this principle. I am delighted to see the hon. member for Essex East back in his seat. We always welcome him and his pleasant smile. I would point out that if those in opposition are going to tell us that Canada's defence policy is related only to a single weapon in its experimental stages, which supplements a defence system which is as comprehensive as one can be in relation to that which we can afford, then it brings this debate into proper perspective.
Let us look at the history of Bomarc. First of all, we know that there were several experimental stages of the earlier edition, the model A, There were some 82 tests before it was successful. Because of certain limitations in our air defence we extended our support for NORAD by having two bases built in Canada. Through negotiations with the United States we contracted for those bases. We then agreed to take a certain number of Bomarc B's. It should be remembered, that in its early stages it may not be entirely satisfactory. This, of course, we do not deny, but we have an insurance for an amount of $15 million placed on this one particular weapon.
This is the point I should like to bring home to the house. We hear repeatedly, particularly from the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer >, expressions of regret that the government decided to cancel the Arrow contract. This is a debate that will long be remembered in this chamber. Certainly, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has never had any firm views on this subject. Certainly, the Leader of the Opposition has never at any time yet agreed with the views of the hon. member for Trinity. It was obvious to this house that the Arrow was not going to be a satisfactory weapon for the air defence of Canada. It was then up to this government to provide an alternative and
Continental Air Defence Policy to supplement the air squadrons, so this $15 million insurance item was put up for the test, to complement our air defence.
Would the hon. member permit a question?

Yes, when I have concluded my remarks. Having occupied most of the time of this house in debates on defence, you can wait your turn.
So, having now in the early stages put up this $15 million out of a total budget of $1,700 million, we see these great defence critics trying to create the impression both in Canada and outside of Canada that Canada is left defenceless. Could anything be more silly, more utterly stupid than that observation by the opposition.
We have also had considerable comment from the Leader of the Opposition and his colleagues on the question of consultation. This, of course, is related to the problems, which they have described, of Canadian sovereignty and the infringement by a foreign country. The Minister of National Defence, who is responsible for the defence of this country to a large degree, gave an itemized account of the various consultations which have taken place, all of which are certainly related to his administration and which were not even conceived by the former government. These were all introduced and initiated by the present government. It seems hardly necessary for me to itemize them all again.
Certainly we have had consultations at the cabinet level; consultations between the House of Commons members and the United States senate and congress; then, through NORAD and through the senior levels of government. I took the time during the recess to ask exactly what consultations at the staff working level, if any, took place prior to the statement read by the minister to the house on Friday. I think it is important because this information would be available to anyone if they took the time to ask for it. The impression has been left that all of a sudden there was a telephone call and our Minister of National Defence then had to make a statement which was dictated by the United States and Canada had no say in it whatever.
Hear, hear.

This is the impression, and the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) says, "hear, hear."
Let us look at the record. First of all, on February 24 representatives of the R.C.A.F. on the higher level met at Washington with the United States air force. On February 28 in Washington, there was a further consultation on the air defence problem, which

Continental Air Defence Policy the R.C.A.F. again attended. On March 1, in Ottawa, a further discussion on exactly the same problem and a team of senior United States air force officers came here to meet with the R.C.A.F. On March 9 there was a further consultation in Ottawa on the same problem.
These are some of the consultations at the working level during the discussion of various changes in the policy of the United States as it might affect Canada. These are actual examples of co-operation that took place between United States and Canadian forces in determining continental defence policy through NORAD. I suggest this is exactly the type of information those in opposition might have checked before they said anything.
My friend, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, widened the debate when he said that this present government had made no useful contribution to the defence of Canada, or words to that effect. I would answer, first, of course that I am going into an area which is beyond the terms of the initial resolution, but since the subject was introduced to such an extent by the minister for Essex East (Mr. Martin) who explored almost every conceivable alley available, and by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate, let us have a look at the record to see what we have done.
Mr. Speaker, I am rising on a point of order.
Sit down.

I am rising on a point of order. The hon. gentleman said that my hon. friend from Essex East had widened the debate. The only person who has taken part in this debate who widened the debate was the Minister of National Defence, who spoke generally about policy without exception being taken by anyone on this side. But when my hon. friend-
Sit down.

Continental Air Defence Policy that a weapon of such precision cannot be put into production after a single test, when it takes years of testing to make a modern aircraft perfectly safe? And incidentally, let me point out that the Avro Arrow had not yet proven itself after a number of tests.
Opposition members would expect American engineers to perform a miracle in successfully firing the Bomarc B at the first test. If the Russians boast of their successes, you may be sure that they never tell about their failures, even though they had many of them before their recent achievements. I do not believe that by reducing the number of bases from 18 to 14, including the two in Canada, the Americans want to show that they no longer have confidence in Bomarc B; I am rather inclined to believe that they tend to direct their efforts towards offensive rather than defensive weapons.
As for us, Canadians, who have always favoured a defensive policy-and it is good that we should stick to it-it is hard to imagine Canada attacking some other country. It is true that the Liberal government of 1939 had seen fit to declare war before London had done so. But I am sure that this government would not do such a thing. Our advantages in keeping Bomarc for our defence lie in the fact that Bomarc B requires little money to provide protection for our industrial centres. And even if Bomarc were to be scrapped in 1970, I am sure that we would have had a good protection during those ten years, at an average cost of $1,500,000 a year.

I am convinced that, as a result of the wisdom of the Department of National Defence and of our alliance with the United States in NORAD, we will always find a way to get adequate protection for Canada.
I am convinced that despite the complaints of the hon. members of the opposition and despite their confusion, Bomarc would be useful to the people of Canada in the event of enemy attack.

speechtext:
For tomorrow, Mr. Speaker, for the period 2.30 to six o'clock we shall have the motion standing in my name, which is a reference to the standing committee on agriculture and colonization to examine into the delivery of grain to feed mills in the prairies, item No. 246 on today's order paper. It will be followed by item No. 239 on today's order paper, which is a resolution in the name of the Minister of Public Works, dealing with an amendment to -the Trans-Canada Highway Act.
At eight o'clock the Minister of Finance will be available to continue the study of the final supplementary estimates. I am not able to forecast the events for Wednesday and Thursday.
At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
